title: Comparison of Cartesian edges with fixed target
statement: Use small quasicategories, coherent triangles and equivalences of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], and Cartesian fibrations and edges of [def-coef-infinity-fibrations]. Let $u:E\to\Delta^1$ be a Cartesian fibration, with endpoint fibres $P=E_0$ and $D=E_1$. For each $d\in D$ choose a $u$-Cartesian edge $c_d:g(d)\to d$ over $0\to1$. If $e:x\to d$ is another $u$-Cartesian edge over $0\to1$, the space of edges $h:x\to g(d)$ in $P$ together with a coherent triangle $c_dh\simeq e$ over the triangle $(0,0,1)$ is contractible, and every such $h$ is an equivalence in $P$. Every $u$-Cartesian edge over a degenerate edge of $\Delta^1$ is an equivalence in its endpoint fibre.

source.place: Higher Algebra (2017), Theorem 2.3.3.23(1), printed pp. 266-268; Converse condition (ii): passage from the canonical Cartesian edge to all Cartesian edges. Agent expansion of the proof; read online 2026-10-17, WANTED archive in report.md. No Stacks tag states this quasicategorical result.

proof.text: Fix $d$, write $y=g(d)$ and $c=c_d$. Specify the comparison space $T$ by the right-pinched coherent-triangle model: an $n$-simplex is a map $\sigma:\Delta^{n+2}\to E$, with vertices ordered $0,\ldots,n,y,d$, whose initial $\Delta^n$ is constant at $x$, whose last edge is $c$, and whose face omitting $y$ is the pullback of $e$ along the monotone map $[n+1]\to[1]$ taking the first $n+1$ vertices to $0$ and the last to $1$. Require its image under $u$ to be the simplex with vertex sequence $(0,\ldots,0,0,1)$. Operators apply a monotone map to the initial block and fix the two last vertices; the restrictions are preserved. Its vertices are exactly triangles with edges $h:x\to y$, $c$ and $e$ over $(0,0,1)$; its higher simplices retain those fixed-edge compatibilities. This is the right-pinched model of the space in the statement, rather than the set of triangle fillers. The edge $h$ lies in $P$ since its whole image in $\Delta^1$ is constant at $0$.

source.place: Remark 2.4.1.9 and the strict slice calculation preceding Proposition 2.4.4.2; explicit right-pinched comparison model.

proof.text: A boundary $\partial\Delta^n\to T$ prescribes, in $\Delta^{n+2}$, the faces omitting each of $0,\ldots,n$. The fixed $e$ prescribes the face omitting $y$; its subfaces prescribe the constant initial face and the required endpoints. Together these are precisely $\Lambda_{n+2}^{n+2}$, the union of every face except the one omitting $d$. Their intersections agree by the simplicial compatibility and the fixed restrictions in Step 1. The final edge is $c$ and the base simplex is $(0,\ldots,0,0,1)$. The horn-Cartesian definition of $c$ therefore gives a filler over that exact base simplex, hence a simplex of $T$ filling the boundary. When $n=0$, the domain is $\Lambda_2^2$, consisting of $c$ and $e$, and this proves nonemptiness as well. Thus $T\to\Delta^0$ lifts all boundaries. It also lifts every horn: first fill the boundary of the missing face (using the boundary result one dimension lower), then fill the resulting full boundary. For a one-dimensional horn first choose the missing vertex by the dimension-zero result. Hence $T$ is Kan.

source.place: Definition 2.4.1.1 and Remark 2.4.1.4, horn formulation; direct boundary-to-outer-horn calculation.

proof.text: Apply [lem-cbc-kan-fibration-fiber-criterion] to the Kan fibration $T\to\Delta^0$. Step 2 makes this a trivial Kan fibration, including the dimension-zero boundary. The cited equivalence between triviality and contractible vertex fibers says that its sole fiber, namely $T$, is contractible. This proves the full space assertion, without first assuming that the edge $e$ is Cartesian; only $c$ was used so far.

source.place: Remark 2.4.1.9 and Proposition 2.4.4.3: contractibility of the strict factorization space; Kan-fibration criterion supplied by the cited node.

proof.text: We now use that $e$ is Cartesian too. For each vertex $z\in P$, apply [lem-coef-infinity-cartesian-mapping-criterion] to $c:y\to d$ and $e:x\to d$. Both lower horizontal arrows are $\operatorname{Map}_{\Delta^1}(0,0)\to\operatorname{Map}_{\Delta^1}(0,1)$, a map between one-point simplicial sets: a simplex in either mapping space is the unique monotone map with the prescribed endpoints. Thus the path-space homotopy pullback in that criterion is just the upper-right mapping space. Also $\operatorname{Map}_E(z,y)=\operatorname{Map}_P(z,y)$ and $\operatorname{Map}_E(z,x)=\operatorname{Map}_P(z,x)$ degreewise: every base simplex all of whose vertices are $0$ is constant. Consequently postcomposition gives weak equivalences $c_*:\operatorname{Map}_P(z,y)\to\operatorname{Map}_E(z,d)$ and $e_*:\operatorname{Map}_P(z,x)\to\operatorname{Map}_E(z,d)$, in particular bijections on components. The endpoint fibers are quasicategories: an inner horn in a fiber lifts against $u$ with constant base simplex and stays in that fiber.

source.place: Proposition 2.4.4.3, specialized to the interval; Remark 2.4.1.9.

proof.text: For any vertex $(h,\tau)$ of $T$, its triangle gives $[c][h]=[e]$ by [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-composition]. Surjectivity of $e_*$ at $z=y$ supplies an edge $k:y\to x$ in $P$ with $[e][k]=[c]$. Associativity gives $[c][h][k]=[c]$ and $[e][k][h]=[e]$. Injectivity of $c_*$ at $z=y$ gives $[h][k]=[1_y]$, and injectivity of $e_*$ at $z=x$ gives $[k][h]=[1_x]$. These equalities are in the homotopy category of $P$: its composition is the restriction of the same canonical composition, since triangles whose vertices lie over $0$ lie wholly in $P$. The cited composition theorem identifies invertible component classes with edges admitting the two inverse-triangle witnesses. Therefore every such $h$ is an equivalence in $P$, for every choice of the coherent triangle.

source.place: Remark 2.4.1.9; explicit cancellation on mapping-space components, using the criterion in Step 4.

proof.text: Finally let $a:v\to w$ be $u$-Cartesian over the identity of $i\in\{0,1\}$. For every $z\in E_i$, the Cartesian mapping criterion has lower row $\operatorname{Map}_{\Delta^1}(i,i)\to\operatorname{Map}_{\Delta^1}(i,i)$, the identity of a point. Every mapping simplex between these endpoint objects lies in $E_i$, as in Step 4. Thus $a_*:\operatorname{Map}_{E_i}(z,v)\to\operatorname{Map}_{E_i}(z,w)$ is a weak equivalence. At $z=w$, surjectivity on components gives $b:w\to v$ in $E_i$ with $[a][b]=[1_w]$. At $z=v$, injectivity and $[a][b][a]=[a]$ give $[b][a]=[1_v]$. The composition theorem supplies the inverse triangles inside $E_i$, so $a$ is an equivalence in its endpoint fiber. This proves the final clause for both endpoints, without assuming that all edges in an endpoint fiber are Cartesian.

source.place: Proposition 2.4.1.5, restricted to an identity base edge; direct derivation from Proposition 2.4.4.3.
